content: Galbanum is an aromatic gum resin derived from specific Persian plant species, primarily Ferula gummosa (synonym galbaniflua) and Ferula rubricaulis. These plants are abundant on the slopes of the mountain ranges in northern Iran. The resin typically appears in hard or soft, irregular lumps that are somewhat translucent and shiny. Occasionally, it is found in separate tears. Its color ranges from light brown to yellowish or greenish-yellow. Galbanum has a disagreeable, bitter taste and a distinctive, musky odor.212. The chemical composition of galbanum includes approximately 8% terpene, about 65% resin (which contains sulfur), around 20% gum, and a very small amount of a colorless crystalline compound known as umbelliferone. Historically, galbanum is one of the oldest known medicinal substances. It is mentioned in the Book of Exodus (30:34) as a sweet spice used in the preparation of a sacred perfume for the tabernacle. However, Rabbi Shelomo ben Yitschak (Rashi) in the 12th century noted that galbanum is bitter and was included in the incense as a symbolic reminder of deliberate and unrepentant sinners. In modern times, galbanum is occasionally used in the production of perfumes. It is the key ingredient responsible for the distinctive and unique scent of the fragrance Must by Cartier. Historically, Hippocrates utilized galbanum in medical treatments, and Pliny the Elder, in his Natural History (Book 24, Chapter 13), attributed remarkable healing properties to it. Pliny even claimed that merely touching galbanum mixed with oil of spondylium was sufficient to kill a serpent. In contemporary medicine, galbanum is rarely prescribed, but when used, it is administered in doses ranging from five to fifteen grains. Its pharmacological effects are consistent with those of substances containing both resin and volatile oils. However, its use in modern medical practice is now largely obsolete.
